title: Boundaries & Difficult Conversations
description: Explore preferences, requests and boundaries through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: A boundary isn't a command
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of preferences, requests and boundaries.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual (2015), interpersonal effectiveness.
nodes.scenario: Ellie and Dev share a flat. Dev occasionally invites guests without warning.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I need notice before people come into our shared space.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I don't want to ask permission every time I see my friends.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm asking for notice, not to choose your friends.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What if plans happen at the last minute?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'll use my room if I need quiet, but we should agree how shared spaces work.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That sounds different from deciding who I'm allowed to invite.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Dev thinks providing notice amounts to requesting permission for every visitor.
Ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself.
Ellie wants to control which friends Dev may see.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself. Ellie wants to control which friends Dev may see. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.

checks.prompt: You are Ellie. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: If you respect me, you won't have anyone round when I'm tired.
options.reply: That sounds different from deciding who I'm allowed to invite.
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: What if plans happen at the last minute?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: I want enough notice to decide whether to use our living room.
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: Can we agree on a message before guests arrive, including how to handle last-minute visits?
options.reply: Yes. We can discuss exceptions when they happen.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

checks.explanation: The first response addresses what can change. Asking about motives may help eventually; it need not be resolved before the concrete issue can be addressed.
checks.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.

nodes.title: Find the evidence
nodes.prompt: Which two statements most directly support the working explanation?
nodes.explanation: The most informative lines reveal what the situation means to the speaker. They suggest that ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself. Other remarks establish circumstances, which can matter without revealing a psychological process.
nodes.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.
nodes.sources: Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual (2015), interpersonal effectiveness.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
A boundary identifies what someone will accept or how they will act. A request invites another person to change their behaviour, and a mutual agreement establishes shared expectations. In a shared home, a good solution must account for both residents' legitimate use of the space.

Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.
nodes.sources: Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual (2015), interpersonal effectiveness.

nodes.explanation: The strongest candidate is ellie is trying to negotiate a shared-space rule while describing what she can do herself. The lower two rankings are more uncertain, and new evidence could reasonably reverse them.
nodes.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.

nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: Can we agree on a message before guests arrive, including how to handle last-minute visits? Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.
nodes.sources: Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual (2015), interpersonal effectiveness.

lessons.takeaway: A request asks somebody to change. A boundary explains what you will do. An agreement sets shared expectations.

nodes.title: Two people, different meanings
nodes.prompt: Which conclusion accounts for both perspectives without confusing an interpretation with a fact?
nodes.explanation: Each character can be responding to a different meaning of the same event. The immediate issue is still observable. Understanding both viewpoints helps explain the conflict without requiring both interpretations to be equally accurate.
nodes.counterexample: Safety and tenancy conditions can justify firmer rules. A self-described boundary is not automatically fair or enforceable.

Both viewpoints matter for understanding the exchange, but neither alone establishes the full cause; address the observable concern as well.

nodes.prompt: What should happen to your working explanation now?
nodes.explanation: Changing a belief requires comparing the new material with what was already known.
